sentences.text: Merryn is thirty-one and she works in fisheries science and she will tell you exactly what is wrong with all of that.
Fifty-eight days of a twelve-year-old with binoculars is not a study.
There is no control, no blind, and an enormous confirmation bias, because on the days when she was expecting the post to be occupied she looked harder at it.
And there is a mechanism problem that she thinks is fatal and that nobody in Porthallow has ever engaged with.
A cormorant does not care about boats.
They are not a food source, they are not a threat, and the fleet at Porthallow is eleven small crabbers that go out at dawn and come back when they are done.

A bird sitting on a post at the end of a wall is sitting there because it is a good post with a good view of the channel and it needs to dry, and it leaves when it is dry, and how long that takes depends on wind and sun and how long it has been in the water.
There is also no reason to think it is one bird.

Merryn has tagged enough of them to know how much they move; the post at Porthallow is a good post and there are several hundred cormorants working that stretch of coast, and the idea that the same individual has been on that pole since her grandmother was a girl is not defensible for a second.
The days a boat is late are days with weather in them.
Weather is also what keeps a cormorant on a post.
A wet bird in still cold air takes a long time to dry.
A wet bird in a breeze is off in twenty minutes.
So the confound is not incidental — it is the strongest single predictor of both variables, and any correlation between late boats and occupied posts falls straight out of it with nothing left over.
That is the whole of it.
She has said it in exactly those words to her uncle, at a table, at nineteen, and her uncle said, "Right," and did not argue, and she has never once managed to make it stick.
